The Daurian ground squirrel (Spermophilus dauricus) is a medium-sized hibernator inhabiting the steppes and grasslands of northern China, Mongolia, and southeastern Russia. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], metabolic measurements reveal a maximum basal oxygen consumption of 182.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 182.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that appears somewhat elevated relative to the species' adult body mass range and may reflect the energetic demands of thermoregulation during the active season. This resting metabolic rate, obtained from post-absorptive individuals during the summer active period, provides a crucial baseline for understanding the species' energy budget throughout its annual cycle. The relatively high metabolic throughput likely supports the rapid somatic tissue deposition required before hibernation onset. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this oxygen consumption level is near the upper limit expected for ground squirrels of comparable size, possibly indicating a particularly high mass-specific metabolic rate in this population.

Female Daurian ground squirrels experience a relatively brief gestation period of 28 days [tg = 28 days] when maintained at a body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a duration that is typical for sciurid rodents of this body size and reflects a pattern of accelerated foetal development consistent with the constraints imposed by a short active season. Following parturition, the altricial neonates are wholly dependent on maternal care. The neonatal body mass averages approximately 5.25 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.25 grams], a modest birth weight that places these pups squarely within the expected range for the genus. This low initial mass is balanced by rapid postnatal growth rates. The suckling juvenile stage persists for a period of 30 days after birth [tx = 30 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions, after which the young begin to emerge from the natal burrow and transition to a solid food diet, achieving nutritional independence from the lactating female.

The species exhibits a life-history strategy geared toward capitalizing on a short growing season and surviving prolonged winter dormancy. Under stable thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], a relatively extended longevity for a rodent of this body size and one that likely reflects the protective benefits of hibernation against extrinsic mortality sources. Female reproductive biology is characterized by a single annual litter. Each breeding event yields between 4 and 8 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 4 and 8 pups per litter], and females typically produce just one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], limiting their total annual reproductive output considerably. This low fecundity is offset by high parental investment in each offspring.

Sexual maturation in Spermophilus dauricus occurs after a substantial developmental delay relative to birth. Under the standard reference body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], young ground squirrels reach puberty at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth], meaning they typically do not breed until the spring following their birth year. This long interval to reproductive maturity is a common feature among hibernating ground squirrels and reflects the need to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for both hibernation survival and subsequent reproduction. The maximum recorded adult body mass for females reaches 264 grams [Wwi = 264 grams], although field studies indicate substantial interpopulation variation, with body weights ranging from 154 to 264 grams depending on local resource availability and habitat quality. Heavier females generally achieve higher overwinter survival rates and produce larger litters.

The population dynamics of this steppe-dwelling sciurid are tightly coupled to seasonal resource pulses and climatic variability across its range. With a single annual litter averaging 5.5 pups [N_R_i = litter averaging 5.5 pups] and one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], the annual reproductive output reaches 5.5 pups per year [Ri = 5.5 pups per year], a modest number that underscores the species' reliance on high adult survival rather than high fecundity for population persistence. Further complicating their demographics, the timing of spring emergence and the consequent onset of the breeding season are highly dependent on snowmelt patterns, which can result in significant year-to-year variation in the length of the active period. Successful recruitment is therefore contingent upon a precise synchronization between parturition and the peak abundance of emergent vegetation and invertebrates, which provide critical resources for the lactating female and her rapidly growing offspring.
